title: Tropical forest responses to climate extremes: an analysis using an individual-based demographic vegetation model
abstract: Abstract. Tropical forests play a crucial role in the global carbon and water cycles, yet their response to the climate extremes remains uncertain. Here, an individual-based demographic vegetation model is used to investigate the effects of warming and drought on ecosystem dynamics across three neotropical sites that span a precipitation gradient. By explicitly resolving plant hydraulic constraints and demographic processes, the study provides a mechanistic understanding of forest responses to climate stressors. The results reveal that warming had the strongest impact on carbon assimilation in the wettest sites (Paracou and Barro Colorado Island). This reduction was primarily driven by a rising vapor pressure deficit, which induced hydraulic failure even in the absence of soil moisture depletion. In contrast, the driest site (Tapajos National Forest) exhibited the highest sensitivity to drought, driven by severe soil moisture depletion. The analysis also shows that the timescale of imposed stress matters: short daily hot-dry events led to weaker impacts due to partial recovery between pulses, whereas yearly-scale warming and drought produced much stronger, persistent reductions in productivity. These findings highlight the site-specific vulnerabilities of tropical forests to climate extremes, where VPD-induced hydraulic stress limits carbon assimilation under warming in moist sites, while soil moisture constraints dominate in drier ecosystems.
problem: Existing climate and vegetation models lack the necessary demographic and ecological resolution to mechanistically predict how tropical forests respond to the separate versus combined effects of atmospheric water demand and reduced rainfall across different timescales.
method: This study uses an individual-based demographic vegetation model to investigate the effects of warming and drought across three neotropical sites by explicitly resolving plant hydraulic constraints and demographic processes to provide a mechanistic understanding of forest responses to climate stressors.
task: The task is to investigate the effects of warming and drought on tropical forest ecosystem dynamics across three neotropical sites using an individual-based demographic vegetation model that explicitly resolves plant hydraulic constraints and demographic processes.
innovation: Using a demographic vegetation model, this study shows that tropical forest vulnerability to climate extremes depends on site-specific conditions and stress duration, with vapor pressure deficit driving decline in wet sites and soil moisture depletion in drier sites.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: BiomeE is a process-based demographic vegetation model developed to simulate complex ecological dynamics within plant communities (Weng et al., 2019). It builds on the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's LM3-PPA model (Weng et al., 2015), sharing core features such as the representation of plant physiology, vegetation demography, resource competition, and the coupled cycles of carbon, nitrogen, and water in ecosystems (Weng et al., 2022).

Soil moisture is represented by a simple bucket model, in which a single root-zone water store is forced by precipitation, evapotranspiration, and drainage; the resulting soil water content and potential provide the lower boundary condition for the hydraulic model.

For this study, BiomeE was configured with a single plant functional type (PFT), representing an evergreen broadleaf tropical tree, initialized from the model's default tropical PFT parameterization Weng et al. (2022) and refined using site-specific trait data from (Longo et al., 2018).

BiomeE was used to simulate annual Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) at each site (Supplementary Figure A1). The simulations were compared with available eddy covariance observations to assess whether the model reproduces basic productivity patterns under ambient conditions.

Barro Colorado Island (BCI) is a 1,560-hectare island located in Gatun Lake, Panama, covered by evergreen broadleaf tropical moist forest.
The GuyaFlux (GYF) tower is located at the Paracou Field Station in French Guiana, within a 400-hectare area of tropical wet forest (Bonal et al., 2008).
The Tapajos National Forest (TNF) is a protected evergreen forest in the Brazilian Amazon, characterized by a closed canopy with an average tree height of 40 meters (Rice et al., 2004).
